rules.title: Basic sentence order
rules.explanation: In neutral word order the verb comes before its object. Putting the object first (我茶喝) is only used for contrast or a topic, so beginners should use Subj. + Verb + Obj.

wrong_example.why: The object is placed before the verb.

rules.source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), HSK 1 grammar points, https://resources.allsetlearning.com/chinese/grammar/HSK_1_grammar_points, accessed 2026-10-03

Putting the object first (我茶喝) is only used for contrast or a topic, so beginners should use Subj. + Verb + Obj. Common mistake: The object is placed before the verb. Keywords: subject verb object SVO word order. Pattern: Subj. + Verb + Obj.

rules.title: Adjective sentences: 很 comes before the adjective
rules.explanation: An adjective can be the predicate by itself, so a plain statement does not need 是 (我很忙). 是 + adjective does exist, but only for emphasis or contrast ('I AM busy, but...'), so do not mark it wrong. The degree word 很 goes before the adjective, not after it.

wrong_example.why: 很 must come before the adjective, not after it.

rules.source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), HSK 1 grammar points, https://resources.allsetlearning.com/chinese/grammar/HSK_1_grammar_points, accessed 2026-10-03

The degree word 很 goes before the adjective, not after it. Common mistake: 很 must come before the adjective, not after it. Keywords: to be shi adjective hen very busy. Pattern: Subj. + 很 + Adj.

rules.title: 都 and 也 go before the verb
rules.explanation: 都 (all) and 也 (also) come after the subject and before the verb. They do not go after the verb.

wrong_example.en: (We are all students, with 都 after 是.)
wrong_example.why: 都 must come before 是, not after it.

rules.source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), HSK 1 grammar points, https://resources.allsetlearning.com/chinese/grammar/HSK_1_grammar_points, accessed 2026-10-03

rules.title: Yes/no questions with 吗
rules.explanation: Add 吗 to the end of a statement to make a yes/no question. Do not put it in the middle.

wrong_example.en: (Do you like drinking tea? with 吗 in the wrong place.)
wrong_example.why: 吗 belongs at the end of the sentence.

rules.source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), HSK 1 grammar points, https://resources.allsetlearning.com/chinese/grammar/HSK_1_grammar_points, accessed 2026-10-03

rules.title: Follow-up questions with 呢
rules.explanation: Put 呢 after a noun or pronoun to ask 'and you?' or 'what about...?'. The word comes first, then 呢.

wrong_example.en: (I am fine, and you? with 呢 first.)
wrong_example.why: 呢 comes after the word, not before it.

rules.title: Question words stay in place
rules.explanation: A Chinese question word takes the place of the answer. It does not move to the front of the sentence like in English.

correct_example.en: What do you want to eat?

wrong_example.why: 什么 should come after the verb, where the answer would be.

rules.source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), HSK 1 grammar points, https://resources.allsetlearning.com/chinese/grammar/HSK_1_grammar_points, accessed 2026-10-03

rules.title: No 吗 with question words
rules.explanation: A question that already has 什么, 谁, 哪儿, 几 or 怎么 does not need 吗.

wrong_example.en: (What is your name? with an extra 吗.)
wrong_example.why: 吗 should not be added to a question that has a question word.

rules.title: 几 needs a measure word
rules.explanation: To ask 'how many', put a measure word between 几 and the noun.

correct_example.en: How many friends do you have?

wrong_example.en: (How many friends? with no measure word.)
wrong_example.why: The measure word 个 is missing.

rules.title: Numbers need a measure word
rules.explanation: Between a number and a noun you need a measure word. 个 is very common, but many nouns have their own measure word (一本书, 一杯水).

wrong_example.en: (I have three apples, no measure word.)
wrong_example.why: The measure word is missing.

rules.title: Time words usually go before the verb
rules.pattern: Subj. + Time + Verb  /  Time + Subj. + Verb
rules.explanation: In neutral word order a time expression goes before the main verb: after the subject or at the start of the sentence (我明天去学校). Putting it after the verb or at the end is non-standard; in speech it can be added as an afterthought, but beginners should avoid it.

correct_example.en: I am going to school tomorrow.

wrong_example.why: The time word is placed after the verb; it should come before it.

rules.source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), HSK 1 grammar points, https://resources.allsetlearning.com/chinese/grammar/HSK_1_grammar_points, accessed 2026-10-03

Common mistake: The time word is placed after the verb; it should come before it. Keywords: time words tomorrow yesterday word order. Pattern: Subj. + Time + Verb  /  Time + Subj. + Verb

rules.title: Place goes before the verb with 在
rules.explanation: To say where an action happens, the normal order is 在 + place before the verb (我在家看书). Putting the place after the verb and object (我看书在家) is non-canonical in neutral speech, so teach the standard order.

wrong_example.en: (I read at home, with the place last.)
wrong_example.why: 在 + place must come before the verb.

rules.source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), HSK 1 grammar points, https://resources.allsetlearning.com/chinese/grammar/HSK_1_grammar_points, accessed 2026-10-03

Keywords: zai at location where action happens. Pattern: Subj. + 在 + Place + Verb

rules.title: 在 means 'be at', 有 means 'there is'
rules.pattern: Thing + 在 + Place  /  Place + 有 + Thing
rules.explanation: Use 在 to say where something is. Use 有 to say that something exists in a place; the place comes first.

correct_example.en: There are many students in the school.

wrong_example.en: (In the school are many students, with 在.)
wrong_example.why: 有, not 在, says that something exists.

rules.source_point: Expressing existence in a place with 'zai'; Expressing existence with 'you'

rules.title: Negate 有 with 没有
rules.explanation: The negative of 有 is 没有 (or just 没). Never say 不有.

correct_example.en: I do not have any money.

wrong_example.why: 不 cannot be used to negate 有.

rules.source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), HSK 1 grammar points, https://resources.allsetlearning.com/chinese/grammar/HSK_1_grammar_points, accessed 2026-10-03

rules.title: 不 vs 没(有)
rules.pattern: 不 + Verb  /  没(有) + Verb (+ 过)
rules.explanation: 不 commonly negates habitual, general, present/future or willing (volitional) situations. 没(有) commonly negates an event that did not happen or has not happened yet. 'Never done it' uses 没(有) + Verb + 过.

correct_example.en: I have never been to Beijing.

wrong_example.why: 不 cannot be used with 过; use 没(有) for 'have never'.

rules.source_point: Comparing 'bu' and 'mei'; Negation of past actions with 'meiyou'

rules.title: 不 (太) before adjectives
rules.explanation: 不 is the normal way to negate an adjective (不冷, 不太冷). 没 is for events, and it does not combine with a degree word such as 很.

correct_example.en: It is not very cold today.

wrong_example.why: 没 cannot be used together with 很 before an adjective; use 不太.

rules.source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), HSK 1 grammar points, https://resources.allsetlearning.com/chinese/grammar/HSK_1_grammar_points, accessed 2026-10-03

rules.title: Verbal 了 goes right after the verb
rules.explanation: 了 right after a verb marks a bounded, completed event, often with a quantity (我吃了一个苹果). It is not simply a past-tense marker, and it never goes before the verb. Sentence-final 了 is different (see the 了 comparison rule).

correct_example.pinyin: Wǒ chī le yī gè píngguǒ.

wrong_example.pinyin: Wǒ le chī yī gè píngguǒ.
wrong_example.en: (I le eat an apple, with 了 before the verb.)
wrong_example.why: 了 is placed before the verb.

rules.source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), HSK 1 grammar points, https://resources.allsetlearning.com/chinese/grammar/HSK_1_grammar_points, accessed 2026-10-03

Keywords: le completed action finished. Pattern: Subj. + Verb + 了 + Obj.

rules.title: 了 at the end for a new situation
rules.explanation: Put 了 at the end of the sentence to show a change or a new situation. In 'not any more' sentences 了 also goes at the end.

correct_example.en: I do not want to eat any more.

wrong_example.why: 了 must be at the end of the sentence.

rules.title: 的 for possession: owner first
rules.explanation: The owner comes first, then 的, then the thing that is owned.

wrong_example.why: The owner and the thing are in the wrong order.

rules.title: 能 and 会 need a verb
rules.explanation: 能 and 会 are followed by a verb. 会 can sometimes stand alone, but 能 cannot.

wrong_example.why: 能 needs a verb after it.

rules.source_point: Expressing ability or possibility with 'neng'; Expressing a learned skill with 'hui'

rules.title: 想 goes before the verb
rules.explanation: 想 (would like to) comes before the main verb.

correct_example.en: I would like to drink tea.

wrong_example.why: 想 is placed after the verb.

rules.source: Chinese Grammar Wiki (AllSet Learning), HSK 1 grammar points, https://resources.allsetlearning.com/chinese/grammar/HSK_1_grammar_points, accessed 2026-10-03

rules.title: 去 + place first, then the purpose
rules.explanation: To say you go somewhere in order to do something, put 去 + place first and the purpose after it. The reverse order describes two separate actions one after the other (buy things, then go to the shop).

correct_example.en: I go to the shop to buy things.

wrong_example.en: (I buy things, go to the shop.)
wrong_example.why: With this order the shop is no longer the place where you buy things.

rules.source_point: Directional verbs 'lai' and 'qu'; Using the verb 'qu'

rules.title: 太 ... 了 means 'too / so'
rules.explanation: 太 + adjective + 了 means 'too ...' or 'so ...'. Do not add 很 to it.

wrong_example.why: 很 and 太 should not be used together.

rules.title: Dates go from big to small
rules.explanation: Say the month first, then the day. The bigger unit comes before the smaller one.

correct_example.pinyin: Jīntiān shì shí yuè wǔ hào.

wrong_example.pinyin: Jīntiān shì wǔ hào shí yuè.
wrong_example.why: The day is placed before the month.

rules.title: Age uses 岁, not 有
rules.explanation: Say someone's age with number + 岁. 有 + age (有五岁了) appears in speech only for emphasis, so beginners should not use 有 here.

correct_example.en: My daughter is five years old.

wrong_example.why: 有 should not be used to give an age.

rules.title: 是……的 stresses how, when or where
rules.explanation: 是……的 is an emphasis construction for the time, place or manner of an event you already know about. It is not needed for every past event, and 是 can be dropped in positive sentences. In the usual form 的 closes the sentence.

wrong_example.why: The final 的 is missing.

rules.title: The subject can be left out
rules.explanation: When the subject is clear from context, Chinese often leaves it out (昨天去了商店). Do not mark such a sentence as wrong just because it has no subject.

rules.title: 二 vs 两 before measure words
rules.explanation: Before a measure word use 两, not 二. 二 is for counting and for numbers.

wrong_example.why: 二 is used before a measure word.

rules.title: 离 for distance
rules.pattern: Place 1 + 离 + Place 2 + 很 + 近/远
rules.explanation: To say how far two places are, put 离 between them. The first place is the starting point.

correct_example.pinyin: Wǒ jiā lí xuéxiào hěn jìn.
correct_example.en: My home is close to the school.

wrong_example.pinyin: Wǒ jiā xuéxiào lí hěn jìn.
wrong_example.why: 离 must be placed between the two places.

rules.title: The adjective after 比 has no 很
rules.explanation: In A + 比 + B + adjective, the adjective stands without 很. To add degree, put 更 or 还 before it, or 一点 or 多了 after it (他比我高一点).

wrong_example.why: 很 cannot be used in a 比 sentence.

rules.title: 更 and 最 are degree words before adjectives
rules.explanation: 更 (even more) and 最 (most) go directly before an adjective, in the same place as 很. An adjective takes only one degree word, so 最很 or 很更 is wrong.

wrong_example.why: 最 and 很 should not be used together.

rules.explanation: To do something for someone, put 给 + the person before the verb.

rules.title: 一起 goes before the verb
rules.explanation: 一起 (together) comes before the verb.

correct_example.en: Let us go to the shop together.

wrong_example.why: 一起 is placed after the verb.

rules.title: 一下 comes after the verb
rules.explanation: Put 一下 after the verb to make the action short and light.

wrong_example.why: 一下 is placed before the verb.

rules.title: 得 comes right after the verb

rules.explanation: To say how well someone does something, 得 sits right after the verb. With an object, either repeat the verb (他说汉语说得很好) or move the object before the verb (他汉语说得很好). 得 never goes after the object.

rules.title: Describing phrase + 的 + noun
rules.explanation: A phrase that describes a noun goes before the noun and is joined to it with 的.

rules.title: 这/那 + (number) + measure word
rules.explanation: In standard Chinese, 这 and 那 are followed by a measure word before the noun (这本书). Some colloquial phrases drop it, but after a number it is always needed (这两本书).

wrong_example.why: The measure word 本 is missing after the number.

rules.title: 可以 goes before the verb; do not stack modals
rules.explanation: 可以 (may / can) comes before the verb. Do not put it together with 能, 会 or 想 in front of the same verb.

wrong_example.why: Two modal verbs (能 and 可以) are stacked; use only one.

rules.title: 了: after the verb vs at the end
rules.explanation: Verbal 了 follows the verb and marks a completed event (我吃了两个苹果). Sentence-final 了 marks a change or new situation (我吃苹果了). Both together mean 'so far' (我吃了两个苹果了). 了 is not a past-tense marker: habits and states do not take it.

correct_example.pinyin: Wǒ chī le liǎng gè píngguǒ le.
correct_example.en: I have eaten two apples so far.

wrong_example.pinyin: Wǒ měi tiān qù le xuéxiào.
wrong_example.why: 了 is not used for a habitual action.

rules.title: The measure word must fit the noun
rules.explanation: Many nouns need their own measure word: 一杯水, 一本书, 一个人. 个 is very common but is not a replacement for all of them.

wrong_example.why: 水 is counted with 杯, not 个.

rules.title: 把 sentences
rules.explanation: 把 puts the object before the verb. The verb needs something after it, such as 完 or 了.

wrong_example.pinyin: Wǒ kàn wán bǎ shū le.

rules.title: How long: 了 + duration
rules.pattern: Verb + 了 + Duration + (的) + Obj.  /  Verb + Obj. + Verb + 了 + Duration
rules.explanation: There are several ways to say how long: put the duration after 了 and before the object (学习了两年汉语), or repeat the verb (学习汉语学习了两年). The duration cannot simply follow the object.

correct_example.pinyin: Wǒ xuéxí le liǎng nián hànyǔ.
correct_example.en: I studied Chinese for two years.

wrong_example.pinyin: Wǒ xuéxí hànyǔ le liǎng nián.
wrong_example.why: The length of time must come right after 了.

rules.title: 再 vs 又 (repeating)
rules.pattern: 再 + Verb  /  又 + Verb + 了
rules.explanation: 再 is for a repeat that has not happened yet: plans, requests and wishes (请再说一次). 又 is for a repeat that has already happened (他又迟到了), and it can also mark a regular recurrence.

wrong_example.why: 又 is not used in requests; use 再.

rules.title: Two actions at once: 一边……一边……
rules.explanation: Put 一边 before each verb to say two actions happen at the same time. 和 joins nouns (我和他), not two full actions.

correct_example.zh: 他一边吃饭，一边看电视。
correct_example.pinyin: Tā yībiān chīfàn, yībiān kàn diànshì.

wrong_example.en: (He eats and watches TV, with 和.)
wrong_example.why: 和 does not join two actions; use 一边……一边…….

rules.title: 如果 sets the condition; the result uses 就
rules.explanation: 如果 starts the condition and usually comes first (in speech it can follow as an afterthought). The result part often uses 就, not 所以 or 但是.

correct_example.zh: 如果明天下雨，我就不去。
correct_example.pinyin: Rúguǒ míngtiān xiàyǔ, wǒ jiù bù qù.
correct_example.en: If it rains tomorrow, I will not go.

wrong_example.zh: 如果明天下雨，所以我不去。
wrong_example.pinyin: Rúguǒ míngtiān xiàyǔ, suǒyǐ wǒ bù qù.
wrong_example.en: (If it rains tomorrow, so I will not go.)
wrong_example.why: 所以 belongs with 因为, not 如果; use 就 in the result.

rules.title: 越来越 means 'more and more'
rules.explanation: 越来越 means 'more and more'. Do not add 很 to it.

correct_example.en: The weather is getting colder and colder.

wrong_example.why: 很 should not be used with 越来越.

rules.title: 让 + person + verb
rules.explanation: 让 means 'let' or 'ask someone to'. The person comes right after 让, then the verb.

correct_example.en: Mom asks me to go to the shop.

wrong_example.why: The person must come after 让.

rules.title: 还是 in questions, 或者 in statements
rules.explanation: 还是 offers a choice in a question and is the normal form there. 或者 is used in statements ('either ... or').

correct_example.en: Do you want tea or coffee?

wrong_example.en: (You drink tea or coffee, with 或者 in a question.)
wrong_example.why: 还是, not 或者, is used in a choice question.

rules.title: Adjective + 的 + noun
rules.explanation: When an adjective with 很 describes a noun, put 的 between the adjective and the noun.

rules.title: 就 (early) vs 才 (late) before the verb
rules.pattern: Time + 就 + Verb  /  Time + 才 + Verb
rules.explanation: 就 and 才 go after the time expression and before the verb. 就 suggests early or quick; 才 suggests late or slow, and in the 'not until' sense it is normally not used with sentence-final 了.

correct_example.pinyin: Tā liù diǎn jiù qǐchuáng le.
correct_example.en: He got up as early as six.

wrong_example.why: 才 and the time are in the wrong order; the time comes first.

rules.title: 的, 地 and 得
rules.pattern: Modifier + 的 + Noun  /  Adverb + 地 + Verb  /  Verb + 得 + Complement
rules.explanation: 的 links a describing word to a noun (红色的车). 地 links an adverb to a verb (慢慢地走). 得 links a verb to its complement (跑得很快). All three sound like 'de', so they cannot be told apart in Pinyin.

wrong_example.why: After a verb the complement marker is 得, not 的.

rules.title: Direction words 来 and 去 after verbs
rules.explanation: 来 (toward the speaker) or 去 (away) can follow a verb. If the verb has a place object, the place goes between them: 回家去, not 回去家.

wrong_example.why: The place should come between 回 and 去.
